To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
(1) model selection criteria are not reliable in the true few shot setting and (2) the true few shot ability of LMs is significantly worse than what prior work suggests

(1) cross-validation and minimum-description-length (MDL) selection criteria are ineffective for choosing model prompts and hyperparameters when held-out examples are not available (2) both criteria often select models that perform worse than randomly-selected models (3) these results hold even if we account for our uncertainty about a model's true few-shot performance and even if we vary the number of held-out examples used for selection and the amount of computation used for selection
model selection is hard in the few-shot setting and that prior work significantly exaggerated the few-shot ability (i.e., performance with a small amount of data) of LMs.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the ability of language models to perform few-shot learning without access to held-out examples.
how to evaluate the few-shot abilities of language models, and we conclude that it is difficult to do so without access to held-out examples.
how to evaluate and select the best language model for few-shot learning.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the few-shot performance of LMs is overestimated in prior work.
the few-shot ability is still a mystery and needs further investigation.
LMs do not perform well in the true few shot setting, but this is a very hard setting to achieve in practice.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the few-shot ability is not as good as it is claimed to be.

, in true few-shot learning, LMs are no better than randomly selected ones, and that we should not be surprised if future work shows that even random selection is better than the current state of the art.
we find it hard to select a model that works well on a task when we have only a few examples to work with, even if we are given a lot of computation.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the few-shot ability demonstrated by LMs in prior work was likely inflated by the use of held-out examples during model selection.
the few-shot ability and robustness of LMs are still far from satisfactory.
, when held-out examples are not available, we should be more careful in interpreting few-shot performance of LMs.
